core_concept_tested: Weighted percentage returns with linear portfolio allocation constraints
mental_trigger: When two components have a fixed ratio (Bonds : Gold = 1 : 4), combine them into a single composite asset with weighted return (1*6% + 4*8%)/5 = 7.6% and apply Alligation against Stocks (10%).
speed_shortcut: Composite rate of (Bonds+Gold) in 1:4 ratio is (6+32)/5 = 7.6%. Overall rate is 8.2%. By Alligation between Stocks (10%) and (B+G) (7.6%): weight of (B+G) is (10 - 8.2)/(10 - 7.6) = 1.8/2.4 = 3/4 of 100000 = 75000. Bonds = 1/5 of 75000 = 15000; 6% of 15000 = 900.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Do not report the bond principal (15000) instead of the bond gain (900). Always re-read the final noun phrase in TITA questions.

verification_notes: Let X = a and Y = 3b - 3c. Then X - 2Y = 4 and 6X + Y = 50. Solving gives X = 8, Y = 2. Target 2a + 3b - 3c = 2X + Y = 18.
core_concept_tested: Block variable substitution in underdetermined 3-variable linear systems
mental_trigger: When 2 equations have 3 variables (a, b, c) and the coefficients of b and c maintain a constant ratio (-6:6 = 3:-3 = -1:1), collapse (3b - 3c) into a single block variable Y.
first_principles_method: Define Y = 3b - 3c. The system becomes a - 2Y = 4 and 6a + Y = 50. Multiply the second equation by 2 and add: 13a = 104 => a = 8, Y = 2. Thus 2a + Y = 16 + 2 = 18.
speed_shortcut: Set c = 0 immediately (since the system holds for all real b, c satisfying the linear relation). Solve a - 6b = 4 and 6a + 3b = 50 => a = 8, 3b = 2 => 2a + 3b = 18.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Never waste time trying to solve for b and c individually; in indeterminate systems, setting one free variable to 0 is valid whenever the target expression is invariant.

verification_notes: P(-3,-2), Q(1,-5), R(9,1). In parallelogram PQRS, S = P + R - Q = (5, 4). Line SQ passes through Q(1,-5) and S(5,4). Setting y = 0 gives a = 1 + 5*(4)/9 = 29/9.
core_concept_tested: Parallelogram diagonal midpoint invariance and section formula for x-intercept
mental_trigger: When 3 vertices of parallelogram PQRS are given in cyclic order, immediately use P + R = Q + S => S = P + R - Q.
first_principles_method: Midpoint of PR equals midpoint of QS, so S = (-3 + 9 - 1, -2 + 1 - (-5)) = (5, 4). The equation of line QS through (1, -5) and (5, 4) is (y + 5)/(4 + 5) = (x - 1)/(5 - 1). At y = 0, (x - 1)/4 = 5/9 => x = 29/9.
speed_shortcut: Since y_Q = -5 and y_S = 4, the x-axis (y = 0) divides segment QS internally in the ratio 5 : 4. Thus a = (5*x_S + 4*x_Q)/(5 + 4) = (5*5 + 4*1)/9 = 29/9.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Preserve cyclic vertex order P-Q-R-S: opposite vertices are (P, R) and (Q, S), NOT (P, Q).

verification_notes: SI for 3.5 years = 18960 - 13920 = 5040 => SI per year = 1440. Principal P = 13920 - 3(1440) = 9600. Annual rate R = 1440/9600 = 15%. Semi-annual rate = 7.5% for 4 periods: CI = 9600*(1.075^4 - 1) = 3220.50 -> nearest to 3221.
core_concept_tested: Simple interest rate extraction followed by semi-annual compound interest accumulation
mental_trigger: Difference of two SI amounts divided by difference of times gives annual SI; then for 4 periods at 7.5%, use two successive 2-period effective rates: 7.5 + 7.5 + 0.5625 = 15.5625%, then 15.5625*2 + (15.5625)^2/100 = 33.547%.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: 6 years and 6 months is 6.5 years (not 6.6 years). Compounding every 6 months for 2 years means 4 compounding periods at 7.5%, not 2 periods at 15%.

verification_notes: For x in [n, n+1) with n in {3, 4, 5}, [x]^2 = n^2, so [x^2] = n^2 iff n^2 <= x^2 < n^2 + 1, i.e., n <= x < sqrt(n^2 + 1). At x = 6, [36] = 36. Thus S = [3, sqrt(10)) U [4, sqrt(17)) U [5, sqrt(26)) U {6}. Option (A) is a valid subset of S.
core_concept_tested: Greatest Integer Function (GIF) step intervals for [x^2] = [x]^2
mental_trigger: For x > 0 with [x] = n, [x^2] = [x]^2 holds if and only if n^2 <= x^2 < n^2 + 1, i.e., x in [n, sqrt(n^2 + 1)) with a strict open right bracket!
first_principles_method: Decompose [3, 6] into [3, 4), [4, 5), [5, 6), and {6}. On [n, n+1), [x] = n so [x^2] = n^2 requires x^2 < n^2 + 1 => x in [n, sqrt(n^2+1)). Hence S = [3, sqrt(10)) U [4, sqrt(17)) U [5, sqrt(26)) U {6}. Only Option (A) avoids the excluded right endpoints sqrt(10), sqrt(17), sqrt(26).
speed_shortcut: Test x = sqrt(10): [x^2] = 10 while [x]^2 = 3^2 = 9 (fails!). This immediately eliminates Options (C) and (D). Test x = sqrt(26.5) in Option (B): [x^2] = 26 != 25 (fails!). Only Option (A) remains.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: The right endpoint sqrt(n^2 + 1) is ALWAYS open because at x = sqrt(n^2 + 1), x^2 jumps to n^2 + 1 while [x] is still n.

verification_notes: x^2 - 5x + k = 0 has integer roots r1, r2 with r1 + r2 = 5 and r1*r2 = k >= 0. Since k >= 0, both roots are non-negative integers summing to 5: (0,5)->k=0, (1,4)->k=4, (2,3)->k=6. Total 3 values.
core_concept_tested: Vieta root-coefficient relations and non-negative integer constraints
mental_trigger: When sum of integer roots is fixed (r1 + r2 = 5) and product k = r1*r2 >= 0, enumerate unordered non-negative integer pairs summing to 5.
first_principles_method: By Vieta relations, r1 + r2 = 5 and r1*r2 = k. Since k >= 0 and r1 + r2 > 0, both r1, r2 >= 0. Unordered integer pairs are {0, 5} (k = 0), {1, 4} (k = 4), and {2, 3} (k = 6), giving 3 values of k.
speed_shortcut: Discriminant 25 - 4k must be a perfect square s^2 with 0 <= 4k <= 25 and s odd: s in {1, 3, 5} => k in {6, 4, 0} -> 3 values.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: The phrase non-negative integer values of k includes k = 0 (roots 0 and 5). Forgetting k = 0 gives the trap answer 2.

verification_notes: Total CP of 13 chairs = 1300. Total SP for 26% profit = 1300 * 1.26 = 1638. Customer pays discounted price of 12 chairs = 12 * 0.78 * MP = 1638 => MP = 1638 / 9.36 = 175.
core_concept_tested: Successive multiplying factors combining discount and free-article promotional schemes
mental_trigger: Giving 13 articles for the price of 12 multiplies effective SP per article by 12/13. Apply: CP * (1 + Profit%) = MP * (1 - Discount%) * (12/13).
first_principles_method: For 13 chairs, total CP = 13 * 100 = 1300 and required revenue = 1300 * 1.26 = 1638. Revenue equals 12 chairs at 22% discount: 12 * (0.78 * MP) = 1638 => MP = 175.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Giving 13 chairs for the price of 12 means the shopkeeper parts with 13 chairs (denominator is 13, not 12).

verification_notes: 5 sandwiches * 4 breads * 2 sizes * (6C0 + 6C1 + 6C2 sauces) = 40 * (1 + 6 + 15) = 40 * 22 = 880.
core_concept_tested: Fundamental multiplication rule with 'up to k' combination cases
mental_trigger: 'Optionally add up to 2 out of 6 sauces' means 0, 1, or 2 sauces: C(6,0) + C(6,1) + C(6,2) = 1 + 6 + 15 = 22.
first_principles_method: Choices for sandwich type = 5, bread = 4, size = 2. For sauces, 'up to 2' includes 0 sauces (1 way), 1 sauce (6 ways), or 2 sauces (15 ways), totaling 22 ways. Total orders = 5 * 4 * 2 * 22 = 880.
speed_shortcut: Since 1 + 6 + 15 = 22 is a multiple of 11, the total number of orders must be divisible by 11. Among (A) 600, (B) 840, (C) 880, (D) 800, only 880 is divisible by 11!
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Forgetting the 0-sauce case ('Optionally... up to 2') gives 40 * 21 = 840 (distractor B).

verification_notes: For base b = 1/4 in (0, 1), log_{1/4}(A) >= 0 requires 0 < A <= 1. Here A = n^2 - 7n + 11 <= 1 => (n-2)(n-5) <= 0. Under strict < 1, integers in (2,5) are n=3,4 (2 integers), while under <= 1 (or |n^2-7n+11|), n=2 and n=5 give A=1 (2 integers). Both routes yield 2.
core_concept_tested: Logarithmic inequality direction reversal for base in (0, 1) and argument positivity domain
mental_trigger: When log base is between 0 and 1 (here 1/4), reverse the inequality sign AND enforce argument > 0.
first_principles_method: Flipping the inequality for base 1/4 < 1 gives n^2 - 7n + 11 < 1 => n^2 - 7n + 10 < 0 => (n - 2)(n - 5) < 0, which has 2 integers (n = 3, 4); if the inequality in the original exam was >= 0, then 0 < n^2 - 7n + 11 <= 1 yields n in {2, 5}, which also gives exactly 2 integers.
speed_shortcut: Since base 1/4 < 1 bounds the upward-opening parabola n^2 - 7n + 11 from above, the solution set is bounded (eliminating D) and narrow around vertex 3.5, giving 2 integers (Option B).
boundary_conditions_and_traps: If you forget to flip the inequality sign for base 1/4 < 1, you get n^2 - 7n + 10 > 0, leading to the trap answer (D) infinite.

core_concept_tested: Sum of squares formula vs arithmetic progression sum in exponential inequalities
mental_trigger: (a_k)^k with a_k = 3^k produces exponent k^2; equate base-3 exponents using sum(k^2) = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
first_principles_method: Compare exponents of 3: LHS = 20*21*41/6 = 2870. RHS = sum_{j=1}^m (20 + j) = 20m + m(m+1)/2 = m(m+41)/2. We need m(m+41) > 5740. Testing m = 57 gives 57*98 = 5586; testing m = 58 gives 58*99 = 5742 > 5740.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Strict inequality (<) means even if LHS == RHS, you would need the next integer; here 58*99/2 = 2871 exceeds 2870 by exactly 1.

verification_notes: For y = 3, x in {4..10} (7 pairs); y = 4, x in {5..9} (5 pairs); y = 5, x in {6..8} (3 pairs); y = 6, x in {7} (1 pair). Total = 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 16.
core_concept_tested: Lattice point counting in triangular inequality regions
mental_trigger: Slice by the smaller integer variable y >= 3: for each y, x ranges from y+1 to 13-y, so count is (13 - 2y) decreasing by 2 each step.
first_principles_method: For each integer y >= 3, x satisfies y + 1 <= x <= 13 - y, giving (13 - 2y) solutions whenever 2y < 13 (i.e., y in {3, 4, 5, 6}). Summing gives 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 16.
speed_shortcut: Sum of first 4 odd numbers (1 + 3 + 5 + 7) = 4^2 = 16.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Notice x > y is strict while y >= 3 is weak, and x + y < 14 means x + y <= 13 for integers.

verification_notes: Radius R = 6*sqrt(2). In isosceles triangle PCQ with angle PQC = 45 deg, perp distance d1 = R*sin(45) = 6 cm and chord PQ = 12 cm. Since d1:d2 = 3:2, d2 = 4 cm. Half-chord of SR = sqrt(72 - 16) = 2*sqrt(14) => SR = 4*sqrt(14). Area of trapezium PQRS = (1/2)*(12 + 4*sqrt(14))*(6 + 4) = 20(3 + sqrt(14)).
core_concept_tested: Parallel chords on opposite sides of a circle center and trapezium area
mental_trigger: Separated by a diameter means the two parallel chords lie on opposite sides of center C, so trapezium height h = d1 + d2 (not |d1 - d2|).
first_principles_method: In triangle CPQ, CP = CQ = 6*sqrt(2) and angle PQC = 45 deg, so angle PCQ = 90 deg, distance d1 = 6, and PQ = 12. From d1 : d2 = 3 : 2, d2 = 4. Then SR = 2*sqrt((6*sqrt(2))^2 - 4^2) = 4*sqrt(14). Since PQ and SR are separated by a diameter, height = d1 + d2 = 10, so Area = 0.5*(12 + 4*sqrt(14))*10 = 20(3 + sqrt(14)).
speed_shortcut: Once d2 = 4 and R^2 = 72 give sqrt(72 - 16) = sqrt(56) = 2*sqrt(14), only Options (A) and (C) contain sqrt(14); since h = 6 + 4 = 10 (not 6 - 4 = 2), Option (A) with factor 20 wins.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Taking height as d1 - d2 = 2 instead of d1 + d2 = 10 gives the trap answer (C) 4(3 + sqrt(14)).

core_concept_tested: Two-component linear mixture / alligation
mental_trigger: Subtract fixed component A (1200) first, then apply Alligation on the remaining 20 shares at average price 2100/20 = 105 between B (90) and C (150).
speed_shortcut: If all 20 shares were C (150), value would be 3000. Excess = 3000 - 2100 = 900. Each swap from C to B saves 60, so B = 900 / 60 = 15.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: None; straightforward 20-second sitter.

verification_notes: f_min = 8c - 4c^2 (at x = 2c) and g_max = 9c^2/4 - 2c (at x = 3c/2). Inequality 8c - 4c^2 > 9c^2/4 - 2c <=> 25c^2/4 - 10c < 0 <=> 0 < c < 8/5. Only c = 1/2 lies in (0, 1.6).
core_concept_tested: Vertex extrema of upward and downward opening parabolas
mental_trigger: Minimum of x^2 + bx + d is d - b^2/4; maximum of -x^2 + bx + d is d + b^2/4.
first_principles_method: Complete the square: f(x) = (x - 2c)^2 + 8c - 4c^2 has min 8c - 4c^2; g(x) = -(x - 1.5c)^2 + 2.25c^2 - 2c has max 2.25c^2 - 2c. Solving 8c - 4c^2 > 2.25c^2 - 2c gives 6.25c^2 < 10c => 0 < c < 1.6. Hence c = 1/2.
speed_shortcut: For any negative c, 8c - 4c^2 < 0 while 2.25c^2 - 2c > 0, immediately eliminating (B) and (C). Between c = 2 and c = 1/2, at c = 2, f_min = 0 < g_max = 5, so c = 1/2 wins.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Watch the sign of the squared term when completing the square on g(x) = -x^2 + 3cx - 2c.

verification_notes: Total time = 180 min in 4 AP parts starting at t1 = 30 => times are 30, 40, 50, 60 min. Speeds: 960, 960+d, 960+2d, 960+3d m/min. Total dist = 180*960 + 320d = 224000 => d = 160 m/min. 4th part dist = (960 + 480)*60 = 86400 m.
core_concept_tested: TSD with speeds and times both in Arithmetic Progression
mental_trigger: Convert 224 km to 224000 m and 3 hours to 180 minutes immediately so units match 960 m/min and 30 min.
speed_shortcut: Base distance at constant speed 960 m/min for 180 min is 172800 m. Extra distance = 224000 - 172800 = 51200 m over (0*30 + 1*40 + 2*50 + 3*60) = 320 d-units => d = 160 => s4*t4 = 1440*60 = 86400.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Do not assume average speed equals the arithmetic mean of the 4 speeds because the time intervals (30, 40, 50, 60) are unequal.

verification_notes: Allowed non-zero digits excluding squares {1,4,9} are {2,3,5,6,7,8}. Since only one digit is prime, the other two must be {6, 8}, and the smallest prime is 2. Minimum 3-digit number is N = 268 = 2^2 * 67^1, which has (2+1)(1+1) = 6 factors.
core_concept_tested: Digit classification constraints and prime-factorization divisor count d(N)
mental_trigger: Filter digits 1..9 by removing squares {1, 4, 9}, leaving primes {2, 3, 5, 7} and composites {6, 8}.
first_principles_method: Non-zero digits not perfect squares: {2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8}. Four are prime ({2, 3, 5, 7}) and only two are non-prime ({6, 8}). Since N has 3 distinct digits and only one prime, N must use both 6 and 8 plus one prime. To minimize N, pick prime 2 in hundreds place: N = 268 = 4 * 67 = 2^2 * 67. Number of factors = 3 * 2 = 6.
speed_shortcut: Once composites are forced to be {6, 8}, smallest hundreds digit is 2 => 268 = 4 * 67 => 3 * 2 = 6 factors.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Remember 1 is a perfect square (1^2 = 1) and is NOT prime.

verification_notes: Initial 13x : 9x (sum 22x); after internal transfer of 21, ratio is 19 : 14 (sum 33y). Equating total: LCM(22, 33) = 66k => 39k - 38k = 21 => k = 21 => shifts become 798 and 588. Adding 3m and 8m gives (798+3m)/(588+8m) = 5/4 => m = 9 => total joined = 11m = 99.
core_concept_tested: Total-invariance under internal transfer and cross-multiplication in ratios
mental_trigger: New students join in ratio 3 : 8, so total new students MUST be a multiple of 3 + 8 = 11 (eliminating B=12). Also internal transfer keeps total students constant!
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Report 11m = 99 (total new students), not m = 9.

core_concept_tested: Rhombus diagonal-side identity d1^2 + d2^2 = 4a^2 and area (1/2)d1*d2
mental_trigger: Whenever rhombus side a and area A are given, use |d1 - d2| = sqrt(4a^2 - 4A) directly without solving for d1 and d2 separately.
first_principles_method: Since diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at 90 deg, (d1/2)^2 + (d2/2)^2 = a^2 => d1^2 + d2^2 = 4a^2 = 5184. Also (1/2)d1*d2 = 396 => 2d1*d2 = 1584. Hence (d1 - d2)^2 = 5184 - 1584 = 3600 => |d1 - d2| = 60.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Memorize |d1 - d2| = 2*sqrt(a^2 - Area) and d1 + d2 = 2*sqrt(a^2 + Area) for any rhombus.

verification_notes: There are 29 odd numbers in {1, 3, ..., 57}, and the sum of the first m odd numbers is m^2. If k is the m-th odd number, (m-1)^2 = 29^2 - m^2 => m^2 + (m-1)^2 = 29^2. By the 20-21-29 Pythagorean triple, m = 21, so k = 2(21) - 1 = 41.
core_concept_tested: Prefix sum of odd numbers (sum = m^2) and the 20-21-29 Pythagorean triple
mental_trigger: Sum of first m odd numbers is m^2; balancing prefix and suffix sums gives (m-1)^2 + m^2 = N^2 = 29^2 -> immediately recall the (20, 21, 29) Pythagorean triple!
first_principles_method: The set {1, 3, ..., 57} has N = (57+1)/2 = 29 terms. Let k = 2m - 1 be the m-th term. Sum of elements < k is (m-1)^2; sum of elements > k is 29^2 - m^2. Equating gives (m-1)^2 + m^2 = 29^2 => m = 21 => k = 2(21) - 1 = 41.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: The m-th odd number is 2m - 1 (41), not 2m (42) or 2(m-1) - 1 (39, distractor C).

verification_notes: Initial acid = 30%. After 20% water replacement: 30% * 0.8 = 24%. After 10% pure acid replacement: 24% * 0.9 + 10% = 31.6%. After 15% water replacement: 31.6% * 0.85 = 26.86%, nearest to 27%.
core_concept_tested: Alternating dilution (water) and enrichment (pure acid) replacement operations
mental_trigger: When replacing with pure acid, track WATER fraction (which gets multiplied by 0.9), or add 10% directly to 0.9 * c_acid; ignore the 200L volume completely!
first_principles_method: Start with c0 = 30%. Step 1 (replace 20% with water): c1 = 30% * 0.8 = 24%. Step 2 (replace 10% with 100% acid): c2 = 24% * 0.9 + 100% * 0.1 = 31.6%. Step 3 (replace 15% with water): c3 = 31.6% * 0.85 = 26.86%, nearest to 27.
speed_shortcut: Never multiply by 200 litres; work purely in percentages: 30 -> 24 -> 31.6 -> 26.86 -> 27.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: In Step 2, replacing 10% of solution with pure acid does NOT multiply acid by 1.10 (which would give 26.4 * 0.85 = 22.44 -> trap D=23).

verification_notes: Total cost per full task: Tarun = 15*2160 = 32400 (cheapest), Varun = 21*2400 = 50400, Arun = 24*2160 = 51840. Employ Tarun for all 10 days (does 10/15 = 2/3 of task, cost 21600). Remaining 1/3 task takes Varun exactly 7 integer days (7/21 = 1/3, cost 7*2400 = 16800) vs Arun 8 days (8/24 = 1/3, cost 8*2160 = 17280). Minimum cost = 21600 + 16800 = 38400.
core_concept_tested: Cost-per-unit-work optimization with integer day-charge step constraints
mental_trigger: Rank workers by Cost per Complete Task (Daily Wage * Days Alone): Tarun (32400) < Varun (50400) < Arun (51840), and max out the cheapest worker for all 10 days.
first_principles_method: To minimize cost within 10 days, employ Tarun (lowest cost per unit work: 32400/task) for the maximum 10 days, completing 10/15 = 2/3 of the task for Rs 21600. For the remaining 1/3 task, Varun needs exactly 7 days (7/21 = 1/3) costing 7*2400 = 16800, whereas Arun needs 8 days (8/24 = 1/3) costing 8*2160 = 17280 (and mixing them requires partial days billed as full days, costing >= 17040). Thus minimum total cost = 21600 + 16800 = 38400.
speed_shortcut: Tarun 10 days (2/3 work, Rs 21600) + Varun 7 days (1/3 work, Rs 16800) = Rs 38400 with zero wasted partial-day billing.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Choosing Arun over Varun because Arun has a lower daily wage (2160 vs 2400) is a classic trap: Arun is slower (24 days vs 21 days), so Arun costs 17280 for 1/3 work -> 38880 (distractor D).

verification_notes: 40% girls and 60% boys left => G and B are multiples of 5, with B > 10 => B >= 15. Remaining: 0.6G - 0.4B = 8 => 3G - 2B = 40. Smallest multiple of 5 for B > 10 with (2B + 40) divisible by 3 is B = 25, giving G = 30. Total = 25 + 30 = 55.
core_concept_tested: Linear Diophantine equation with percentage integrality and strict lower bound
mental_trigger: 40% (2/5) and 60% (3/5) of people must be integers, so let B = 5b (with b >= 3 since B > 10) and G = 5g.
first_principles_method: Let B = 5b (b >= 3) and G = 5g. Remaining girls = 3g, remaining boys = 2b. Given 3g - 2b = 8 => 3g = 2b + 8. Testing b = 3 (14), b = 4 (16), b = 5 (18 = 3*6 => g = 6). Thus B = 25, G = 30, and B + G = 55.
speed_shortcut: In 3g - 2b = 8 with b >= 3, b must be 2 mod 3 => smallest b >= 3 is b = 5 => g = 6 => 5(5 + 6) = 55.
boundary_conditions_and_traps: Ignoring B > 10 gives b = 2 (B = 10, G = 20, total = 30), violating 'more than 10 boys'.
